Weakly Unitary Zeon Matrices

G. Stacey Staples Note: Email: sstaple@siue.edu Affiliation: Department of Mathematics & Statistics
Southern Illinois University Edwardsville
Edwardsville, IL 62026-1653
USA
Abstract

In this paper, zeon matrix groups are discussed for the first time. Extending the concept of unitary complex matrices (i.e., matrices AA such that A†​A=𝕀A^{\dagger}A=\mathbb{I}) to matrices having entries in the complex zeon algebra ℂ​ℨ\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}, a “zeon dagger” operator †^{\hat{{\dagger}}} is defined and used to declare a zeon matrix Ξ\Xi to be unitary if Ξ†^​Ξ=𝕀\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\mathbb{I}. The unitary zeon matrices of order nn form a subgroup 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n} of all invertible order-nn zeon matrices. A more interesting notion is that of “weak unitarity” of a zeon matrix. In particular, a zeon matrix Ξ\Xi will be said to be weakly unitary if Ξ†^​Ξ=𝕀+Γ\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\mathbb{I}+\Gamma, where Γ\Gamma is a diagonal nilpotent zeon matrix. The weakly unitary matrices of order nn form a group 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n}, of which 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n} is a subgroup. It is further shown that the exponential of a graph’s nilpotent adjacency matrix has a natural orthogonal decomposition into the sum of a weakly unitary zeon matrix and a nilpotent zeon matrix. Eigenvalues of the weakly unitary zeon matrix reveal information about the graph’s cycles and paths.

Keywords: zeons, matrix groups, graph processes, linear operators

1 Introduction

Zeon algebras can be thought of as commutative fermion algebras; i.e., their generators commute and square to zero. They arise as subalgebras of Clifford algebras (of appropriate signature) and have natural applications in combinatorics and graph theory [1, 3, 4].

In this paper, the concept of unitary complex matrices (i.e., matrices AA such that A†​A=𝕀A^{\dagger}A=\mathbb{I}) is extended to matrices over the complex zeon algebra ℂ​ℨ\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}; a “zeon dagger” operator †^{\hat{{\dagger}}} is defined and used to declare a zeon matrix Ξ\Xi to be unitary if Ξ†^​Ξ=𝕀\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\mathbb{I}. The unitary zeon matrices of order nn form a subgroup 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n} of all invertible order-nn zeon matrices A much more interesting notion is that of “weak unitarity” of a zeon matrix. In particular, a zeon matrix Ξ\Xi is said to be weakly unitary if Ξ†^​Ξ=𝕀+Γ\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\mathbb{I}+\Gamma, where Γ\Gamma is a diagonal nilpotent zeon matrix. The weakly unitary matrices 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n} of order nn form a subgroup of 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n}.

The paper is laid out as follows. Essential terminology and background on zeon algebras is presented in Section 1.1. Graph-theoretic results related to zeon algebras are reviewed in Section 1.2, while Section 2.0.2 illustrates how zeon matrix exponentials reveal paths in sequences of graphs.

Motivated by the discussion of zeon path matrices, the notions of unitary and weakly unitary zeon matrices are presented in Section 3, where it is shown that when Φ\Phi is the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph, the matrix exponential 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi), can be decomposed into an orthogonal sum of a weakly unitary matrix and a nilpotent zeon matrix. Further, the weakly unitary matrix and its eigenvalues reveal information about paths and cycles contained in the graph. Writing the nilpotent adjacency matrix Φ\Phi of a graph as the Hadamard product of “fermion adjacency matrices,” an alternative formulation of 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi) is presented, potentially opening a new avenue of potential discovery.

The paper closes with Section 4, in which some avenues for further investigation are suggested.

1.1 Preliminaries

For n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, let ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} denote the complex commutative algebra generated by the collection {ζ{i}:1≤i≤n}\{\zeta_{\{i\}}:1\leq i\leq n\} along with the scalar 1=ζ∅1=\zeta_{\varnothing} subject to the following multiplication rules:

ζ{i}​ζ{j}=ζ{i,j}=ζ{j}​ζ{i}​ for ​i≠j, and\displaystyle\zeta_{\{i\}}\,\zeta_{\{j\}}=\zeta_{\{i,j\}}=\zeta_{\{j\}}\,\zeta_{\{i\}}\,\,\text{ \rm for }i\neq j,\text{ \rm and}
ζ{i}2=0​ for ​1≤i≤n.\displaystyle{\zeta_{\{i\}}}^{2}=0\,\,\text{ \rm for }1\leq i\leq n.

It is evident that a general element u∈ℂ​ℨnu\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} can be expanded as u=∑I∈2[n]uI​ζIu=\displaystyle\sum_{I\in 2^{[n]}}u_{I}\,\zeta_{I}, or more simply as ∑IuI​ζI\sum_{I}u_{I}\zeta_{I}, where I∈2[n]I\in 2^{[n]} is a subset of the nn-set, [n]:={1,2,…,n}[n]:=\{1,2,\ldots,n\}, used as a multi-index, uI∈ℝu_{I}\in\mathbb{R}, and ζI=∏ι∈Iζι\displaystyle\zeta_{I}=\prod_{\iota\in I}\zeta_{\iota}. The algebra ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} is called the (nn-particle) complex zeon algebra.

As a vector space, this 2n2^{n}-dimensional algebra has a canonical basis of basis blades of the form {ζI:I⊆[n]}\{\zeta_{I}:I\subseteq[n]\}. The null-square property of the generators {ζi:1≤i≤n}\{\zeta_{i}:1\leq i\leq n\} guarantees that the product of two basis blades satisfies the following:

ζI​ζJ={ζI∪JI∩J=∅,0otherwise.\zeta_{I}\zeta_{J}=\begin{cases}\zeta_{I\cup J}&I\cap J=\varnothing,\\ 0&\text{\rm otherwise.}\end{cases} (1.1)

It should be clear that ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} is graded. For non-negative integer kk, the grade-kk part of element u=∑IuI​ζIu=\sum_{I}u_{I}\zeta_{I} is defined as

⟨u⟩k=∑{I:|I|=k}uIζI.\langle u\rangle_{k}=\sum_{\{I:|I|=k\}}u_{I}\zeta_{I}.

An inner product is defined on ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} by linear extension of

⟨∑IuI​ζI,ζJ⟩=uJ.\displaystyle\left<\sum_{I}u_{I}\zeta_{I},\zeta_{J}\right>=u_{J}.

The basis blades {ζI:I∈2[n]}\{\zeta_{I}:I\in 2^{[n]}\} form an orthonormal collection with respect to this inner product; thus, any element u∈ℂ​ℨnu\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} can be expanded as u=∑I⟨u,ζI⟩​ζI.\displaystyle u=\sum_{I}\left<u,\zeta_{I}\right>\zeta_{I}. Moreover, an inner product norm is naturally induced on ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} by ‖u‖=⟨u,u⟩1/2\|u\|=\langle u,u\rangle^{1/2}.

It is often convenient to separate the scalar term of a zeon element from the rest of it. To this end, for z∈ℂ​ℨnz\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n} we write ℭ​z=⟨z⟩0\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}z=\langle z\rangle_{0} for the scalar part of zz, and 𝔇​z=z−ℭ​z\mathfrak{D}z=z-\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}z for the dual part of zz. The dual part of any zeon element is always nilpotent; i.e., (𝔇​z)k=0(\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}z)^{k}=0 for some positive integer kk. The least such positive integer is called the index of nilpotency of 𝔇​z\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}z and is denoted by κ⁡(𝔇​z)\kappa(\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}z).

The finite-dimensional algebra is extended to zeon algebras of arbitrary dimension by defining

ℂℨ=span{ζI:I⊂ℕ,Ifinite},\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}={\rm span}\{\zeta_{I}:I\subset\mathbb{N},I\,\text{\rm finite}\},

which we call the infinite-dimensional (complex) zeon algebra.

An element u∈C​Zu\in CZ is uniquely invertible if and only if ℭ​u≠0\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}u\neq 0, and the inverse is given by

u−1=1ℭ​u​∑j=0κ−1(−1)j​(ℭ​u)−j​(𝔇​u)j.u^{-1}=\frac{1}{\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}u}\sum_{j=0}^{\kappa-1}(-1)^{j}(\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}u)^{-j}(\mathfrak{D}u)^{j}.

The maximal ideal consisting of nilpotent zeon elements will be denoted by ℂ​ℨ∘={u∈ℂ​ℨ:ℭ​u=0}{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}}^{\circ}=\{u\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}:\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}u=0\}. The multiplicative Abelian group of invertible zeon elements is denoted by

ℂ​ℨ×=ℂ​ℨ∖ℂ​ℨ∘={u∈ℂ​ℨ:ℭ​u≠0}.{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}}^{\times}=\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}\setminus{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}}^{\circ}=\{u\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}:\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}u\neq 0\}.

1.2 Zeons and Graph Theory

For purposes of the discussion at hand, a graph on nn vertices is an ordered pair G=(V,E)G=(V,E) of sets. Elements of V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\} are the vertices of GG, and elements of EE are unordered pairs of distinct vertices, called the edges of GG. Two vertices vi,vj∈Vv_{i},v_{j}\in V are said to be adjacent if there exists an edge {vi,vj}∈E\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\in E.

A walk (v0,…,vk)(v_{0},\ldots,v_{k}) in a graph GG is a finite sequence of vertices in GG with initial vertex v0v_{0} and terminal vertex vkv_{k} such that there exists an edge {vj,vj+1}∈E\{v_{j},v_{j+1}\}\in E for each 0≤j≤k−10\leq j\leq k-1. A walk of length kk, or kk-walk contains kk edges. A path is a walk in which no vertex appears more than once. A closed walk is a walk whose initial vertex is also its terminal vertex. A cycle is a closed path whose terminal vertex is its initial vertex (i.e., vk=v0v_{k}=v_{0}). A Hamiltonian cycle is an nn-cycle in a graph on nn vertices; i.e., each vertex in the graph appears exactly once (with the exception of the terminal/initial vertex).

Definition 1.1.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph on nn labeled vertices V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\ldots,v_{n}\} and edges EE consisting of unordered pairs of vertices. The nilpotent adjacency matrix of GG is defined as the n×nn\times n matrix Φ=(φi​j)\Phi=(\varphi_{ij}) having entries in ℨn{\mathfrak{Z}_{n}} determined as follows:

φi​j={0{vi,vj}∉E,ζ{j}{vi,vj}∈E.\varphi_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\notin E,\\ \zeta_{\{j\}}&\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\in E.\end{cases}

Modifying Dirac notation, let us define ⟨ζ{i}|\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}| to denote the row vector whose entries are all zero, except the iith column, which is ζ{i}\zeta_{\{i\}}. Similarly, |j⟩|j\rangle will denote the column vector with 11 in the jjth row and zeros elsewhere.

Because the generators of ℨn\mathfrak{Z}_{n} square to zero, a straightforward inductive argument shows that the nonzero terms of ⟨vi|Φk|vj⟩\left<v_{i}|\Phi^{k}|v_{j}\right> are multivectors corresponding to two types of kk-walks from viv_{i} to vjv_{j}: self-avoiding walks (i.e., walks with no repeated vertices) and walks in which viv_{i} is repeated exactly once at some step but are otherwise self-avoiding. For i≠ji\neq j, multiplication by ζ{i}\zeta_{\{i\}} cancels walks of the second type, so that nonzero terms represent paths from viv_{i} to vjv_{j}.

When i=ji=j, walks of the second type are zeroed in the kthk^{\rm th} step when the walk is closed. Hence, terms of ⟨vi|Φk|vi⟩\left<v_{i}|\Phi^{k}|v_{i}\right> represent the collection of kk-cycles based at viv_{i}. We thereby arrive at the following result, as first presented in [5].

Nil-Structure Theorem

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of an nn-vertex graph GG, and let k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. For 1≤i≠j≤n1\leq i\neq j\leq n,

⟨ζ{i}|Φk|vj⟩=∑(w1,…,wk)∈Vk(wk=vj)∧(m≠ℓ⇒wm≠wℓ)ζ(w1,…,wk)=∑I⊆V|I|=k+1ωI​ζI,\left<\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Phi^{k}|v_{j}\right>=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{(w_1,\ldots, w_k)\in V^k}{(w_k=v_j)\wedge(m\ne\ell\Rightarrow w_m\ne w_\ell)}}\zeta_{(w_{1},\ldots,w_{k})}=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{I\subseteq V}{|I|=k+1}}\omega_{I}\zeta_{I},

where ωI\omega_{I} denotes the number of kk-paths from viv_{i} to vjv_{j}. Further, when 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

⟨vi|Φk|vi⟩=∑I⊆V|I|=kωI​ζI,\left<v_{i}|\Phi^{k}|v_{i}\right>=\sum_{\genfrac{}{}{0.0pt}{}{I\subseteq V}{|I|=k}}\omega_{I}\zeta_{I},

where ωI\omega_{I} denotes the number of kk-cycles on vertex set II based at vi∈Iv_{i}\in I.

2 The Nilpotent Adjacency Matrix Exponential

It is worth noting that any square matrix of order mm having entries in ℂ​ℨ∘\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ} must be nilpotent by the pigeonhole principle. For any X∈𝕄m​(ℂ​ℨ∘)X\in\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}), the index of nilpotency of XX is denoted by κ⁡(X)\kappa(X). The exponential of any nilpotent square matrix X∈𝕄m​(ℂ​ℨ∘)X\in\mathbb{M}_{m}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}) can therefore be expressed as the finite sum

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(X)=∑k=0κ⁡(𝔇⁡(X))−1Xkk!.\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{\kappa(\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}(X))-1}\frac{X^{k}}{k!}.

Hence, the following zeon elementary functions of XX can be computed as finite sums:

𝔠​𝔬​𝔰​(X)=12​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​X)+𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(−𝕚​X)),\displaystyle\mathfrak{cos}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\frac{1}{2}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}X)+\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(-\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}X)), 𝔰​𝔦​𝔫​(X)=12​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​X)−𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(−𝕚​X)),\displaystyle\qquad\mathfrak{sin}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\frac{1}{2}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}X)-\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(-\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}X)),
𝔠​𝔬​𝔰​𝔥​(X)=12​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(X)+𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(−X)),\displaystyle\mathfrak{cosh}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\frac{1}{2}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(X)+\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(-X)), 𝔰​𝔦​𝔫​𝔥​(X)=12​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(X)−𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(−X)).\displaystyle\qquad\mathfrak{sinh}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\frac{1}{2}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(X)-\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(-X)).

Letting Φ∈𝕄m​(ℂ​ℨm∘)\Phi\in\mathbb{M}_{m}({\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{m}}^{\circ}) be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on mm vertices, it follows that

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ)=∑k=0κ⁡(Φ)−11k!​Φk=𝕀+Ψ,\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi)=\sum_{k=0}^{\kappa(\Phi)-1}\frac{1}{k!}\Phi^{k}=\mathbb{I}+\Psi,

where Ψ∈𝕄m​(ℂ​ℨm∘)\Psi\in\mathbb{M}_{m}({\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{m}}^{\circ}).

The off-diagonal entries of Ψ\Psi satisfy

⟨ζ{i}|Ψ|j⟩=∑I⊆([n]∖∅)ωI(|I|−1)!​ζI,(i≠j),\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Psi|j\rangle=\sum_{I\subseteq([n]\setminus\varnothing)}\frac{\omega_{I}}{(|I|-1)!}\zeta_{I},\hskip 12.0pt(i\neq j), (2.1)

where ωI\omega_{I} is the number of paths in GG from viv_{i} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. The diagonal entries of Ψ\Psi satisfy

⟨i|Ψ|i⟩=∑I⊆([n]∖∅)ξI|I|!​ζI,\langle i|\Psi|i\rangle=\sum_{I\subseteq([n]\setminus\varnothing)}\frac{\xi_{I}}{|I|!}\zeta_{I}, (2.2)

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of cycles11 1 Edges are regarded as 22-cycles. in GG on vertices indexed by II, and containing viv_{i}.

For these reasons, the matrix Ψ=𝔇​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ)\Psi=\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi) will be referred to as the zeon path matrix of GG.

2.0.1 Elementary Functions and Graph Properties

Lemma 2.1.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a graph on nn vertices with nilpotent adjacency matrix Φ\Phi. Then

  1. 1.

    GG is bipartite if and only if tr⁡𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ)=tr⁡𝔠​𝔬​𝔰​𝔥​(Φ)\tr\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi)=\tr\mathfrak{cosh}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi).

  2. 2.

    GG is Hamiltonian if and only if tr⁡(Φn)≠𝟎\tr(\Phi^{n})\neq\mathbf{0}, which is true if and only if ⟨tr⁡𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ)⟩n≠0\langle\tr\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi)\rangle_{n}\neq 0.

Proof.

A well known result of graph theory is that GG is bipartite if and only if all cycles are of even length, proving 1. Item 2 follows immediately from the Nil-Structure Theorem and the definition of the matrix exponential. ∎

2.0.2 Matrix Exponentials and Graph Processes

Let 𝒢={G1,G2,…,Gm}\mathcal{G}=\{G_{1},G_{2},\ldots,G_{m}\} be a collection of graphs on a common fixed set of nn vertices, and let Φ1,…,Φm\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{m} be their respective nilpotent adjacency matrices. Then, ∃Ψ∈Mat⁡(n,ℂ​ℨn∘)\exists\Psi\in{\rm Mat}(n;{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}}^{\circ}) such that

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ1+⋯+Φm)=𝕀+Ψ.\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi_{1}+\cdots+\Phi_{m})=\mathbb{I}+\Psi.

Let us refer to any sequence of (not necessarily distinct) graphs from 𝒢\mathcal{G} as a graph process on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. In this case, Ψ\Psi represents all paths and cycles in all graph processes on 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

Ψ=∑k=1n∑𝐮=(u1,…,uk)∈[m]k1k!​∏j=1kΦuj.\Psi=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{\mathbf{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{k})\in[m]^{k}}\frac{1}{k!}\prod_{j=1}^{k}\Phi_{u_{j}}.

Moreover, the (ordered) products of nilpotent adjacency matrix exponentials enumerate paths in sequences of graphs. For example,

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ1)​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φ2)=(𝕀+Ψ1)​(𝕀+Ψ2)=𝕀+Ψ1+Ψ2+Ψ1​Ψ2,\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi_{1})\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi_{2})=(\mathbb{I}+\Psi_{1})(\mathbb{I}+\Psi_{2})=\mathbb{I}+\Psi_{1}+\Psi_{2}+\Psi_{1}\Psi_{2},

where Ψ1\Psi_{1} and Ψ2\Psi_{2} enumerate paths and cycles in G1G_{1} and G2G_{2}, respectively, and Ψ1​Ψ2\Psi_{1}\Psi_{2} enumerates paths vi→vj→vkv_{i}\to v_{j}\to v_{k} where vi→vjv_{i}\to v_{j} are paths in G1G_{1} and paths vj→vkv_{j}\to v_{k} exist in G2G_{2}. More formally,

⟨ζ{i}|Ψ1​Ψ2|j⟩\displaystyle\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Psi_{1}\Psi_{2}|j\rangle =∑ℓ=1n⟨ζ{i}|Ψ1|ℓ⟩​⟨ℓ|Ψ2|j⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Psi_{1}|\ell\rangle\langle\ell|\Psi_{2}|j\rangle
=∑ℓ=1n(∑IωI​ζI)​(∑JνJ​ζJ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{I}\omega_{I}\zeta_{I}\right)\left(\sum_{J}\nu_{J}\zeta_{J}\right)
=∑KϖK​ζK,\displaystyle=\sum_{K}\varpi_{K}\zeta_{K},

where for each ℓ\ell, ωI\omega_{I} is the number of paths in G1G_{1} from viv_{i} to vℓv_{\ell} on vertices indexed by II and νJ\nu_{J} is the number of paths in G2G_{2} from vℓv_{\ell} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by JJ. Then ϖK\varpi_{K} is the number of paths having initial vertex viv_{i} and terminal vertex vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by KK in which some number of steps occur initially in G1G_{1} and subsequently in G2G_{2}. Extending the concept by induction, we arrive at the following proposition.

Proposition 2.2.

Let 𝒢→=(G1,…,Gm)\vec{\mathcal{G}}=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{m}) be a sequence of graphs on fixed vertex set VV and let (Φ1,…,Φm)(\Phi_{1},\ldots,\Phi_{m}) be the sequence of nilpotent adjacency matrices associated with 𝒢→\vec{\mathcal{G}}. Defining the matrix Ω\Omega by

Ω=∏j=1m𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(Φj)=∏j=1m(𝕀+Ψj),\Omega=\prod_{j=1}^{m}\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\Phi_{j})=\prod_{j=1}^{m}(\mathbb{I}+\Psi_{j}),

it follows that

⟨ζ{i}|Ω|j⟩=∑KϖK​ζK,\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Omega|j\rangle=\sum_{K}\varpi_{K}\zeta_{K},

where ϖK\varpi_{K} is the number of paths from viv_{i} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by KK in the graph process 𝒢→\vec{\mathcal{G}}. Moreover,

⟨j|Ω|j⟩=∑KξK​ζK,\langle j|\Omega|j\rangle=\sum_{K}\xi_{K}\zeta_{K},

where ξK\xi_{K} is the number of cycles based at vertex vjv_{j} in the graph process 𝒢→\vec{\mathcal{G}}.

Obviously, the collection of matrices ℑn={𝕀+Ψ:Ψ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)}⊂𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\mathfrak{I}_{n}=\{\mathbb{I}+\Psi:\Psi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}}^{\circ})\}\subset\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) forms a multiplicative subgroup of the order-nn invertible zeon matrices, 𝔊n\mathfrak{G}_{n}. The subgroup 𝕚n\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}_{n} motivates our discussion of unitary and weakly unitary zeon matrices.

3 Unitary and Weakly Unitary Zeon Matrices

In order to generalize the concept of the Hermitian conjugate of a complex matrix for use with zeon matrices, it is necessary to find a suitable “zeon dagger operator.” To begin, we define the zeon grade involution of an element u=∑IuI​ζI∈ℂ​ℨu=\sum_{I}u_{I}\zeta_{I}\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z} by u^=∑I(−1)|I|​uI​ζI\hat{u}=\sum_{I}(-1)^{|I|}u_{I}\zeta_{I}. Note that u^^=u\hat{\hat{u}}=u and u​v^=u^​v^\widehat{uv}=\hat{u}\hat{v} for all u,v∈ℂ​ℨu,v\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}. Grade involution extends entrywise to zeon matrices.

As will become evident, the composition of the zeon grade involution with the complex conjugate transpose now provides a suitable operator for defining unitary and weakly unitary zeon matrices.

Definition 3.1.

The zeon dagger operator †^{\hat{{\dagger}}} is defined on 𝕄m×n​(ℂ​ℨ)\mathbb{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) by Ξ†^=Ξ^†\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}={\widehat{\Xi}}^{\dagger}, where Ξ^\widehat{\Xi} is the zeon grade involution of Ξ∈𝕄m×n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}).

For any Ξ∈𝕄m×n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}), it is obvious that the operator †^{\hat{{\dagger}}} satisfies

Ξ†^†^=(Ξ^†)†^=((Ξ^†)^)†=(Ξ†)†=Ξ.{\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=({\widehat{\Xi}}^{\dagger})^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=(\widehat{({\widehat{\Xi}}^{\dagger})})^{\dagger}\\ =(\Xi^{\dagger})^{\dagger}=\Xi.

Moreover, for matrices Ψ,Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Psi,\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}), we have (Ψ​Ξ)†^=Ξ†^​Ψ†^(\Psi\Xi)^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}.

Remark 3.2.

The zeon dagger operator restricts to the ordinary conjugate transpose for scalar matrices; i.e., (ℭ​Ξ)†^=(ℭ​Ξ)†(\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\Xi)^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=(\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\Xi)^{\dagger} for any Ξ∈𝕄m×n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}).

Unitary zeon matrices are now defined in the expected way.

Definition 3.3.

An invertible zeon matrix Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) is said to be (strongly) unitary if

Ξ†^​Ξ=Ξ​Ξ†^=𝕀.\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\Xi\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=\mathbb{I}.

We note that the collection 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n} of unitary matrices in 𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) form a multiplicative group, since 𝕀∈𝔘n\mathbb{I}\in\mathfrak{U}_{n} and for any Ψ,Ξ∈𝔘n\Psi,\Xi\in\mathfrak{U}_{n}, we have

(Ψ​Ξ)†^​(Ψ​Ξ)=Ξ†^​(Ψ†^​Ψ)​Ξ=𝕀.(\Psi\Xi)^{\hat{{\dagger}}}(\Psi\Xi)=\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}(\Psi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi)\Xi=\mathbb{I}.

Necessary and sufficient conditions for a zeon matrix to be unitary are established in the next lemma.

Lemma 3.4.

Let Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}). Then, Ξ=∈𝔘n\Xi=\in\mathfrak{U}_{n} if and only if the matrices C=ℭ​ΞC=\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\Xi and D=𝔇​ΞD=\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}\Xi satisfy the following:

  1. 1.

    C†​C=𝕀C^{\dagger}C=\mathbb{I}, i.e., CC is a unitary complex matrix;

  2. 2.

    D†^​D=𝟎D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}D=\mathbf{0};

  3. 3.

    C†​D=−D†^​CC^{\dagger}D=-D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}C.

Proof.

Letting C=ℭ​ΞC=\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\Xi and D=𝔇​ΞD=\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}\Xi, we see that

Ξ†^​Ξ=(C+D)†​(C+D)\displaystyle\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=(C+D)^{\dagger}(C+D) =C†^​C+C†^​D+D†^​C+D†^​D\displaystyle=C^{\hat{{\dagger}}}C+C^{\hat{{\dagger}}}D+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}C+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}D
=C†​C+C†​D+D†^​C+D†^​D.\displaystyle=C^{\dagger}C+C^{\dagger}D+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}C+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}D.

Clearly, C†​C+C†​D+D†^​C+D†^​D=𝕀C^{\dagger}C+C^{\dagger}D+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}C+D^{\hat{{\dagger}}}D=\mathbb{I} if and only if the conditions in the statement of the lemma are satisfied. ∎

The conditions of Lemma 3.4 are quite restrictive. Relaxing these conditions leads to a subgroup of matrices more useful for matters at hand.

Definition 3.5.

An invertible zeon matrix Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) is said to be weakly unitary if there exists a diagonal nilpotent zeon matrix Γ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)\Gamma\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}) such that

Ξ†^​Ξ=Ξ​Ξ†^=𝕀+Γ.\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Xi=\Xi\Xi^{\hat{{\dagger}}}=\mathbb{I}+\Gamma.

The weakly unitary zeon matrices of order nn clearly form a subgroup 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n} of 𝔊n\mathfrak{G}_{n}, the invertible zeon matrices of order nn. Further, the unitary matrices 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n} are a subgroup of 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n}. We shall refer to 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n} as the weak unitary group of n×nn\times n zeon matrices.

A zeon-valued inner-product is defined on 𝕄m×n​(ℂ​ℨ)\mathbb{M}_{m\times n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) by

⟨ψ,ω⟩†^=Tr⁡(ω†^​ψ)\langle\psi,\omega\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=\Tr(\omega^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\psi) (3.1)

where Tr⁡(Ξ)=1n​tr⁡(Ξ)\Tr(\Xi)=\frac{1}{n}\tr(\Xi) denotes normalized trace of Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}). It follows immediately that every weakly unitary zeon matrix ψ∈𝔚n\psi\in\mathfrak{W}_{n} satisfies ⟨ψ,ψ⟩†^=1+γ\langle\psi,\psi\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=1+\gamma for some γ∈ℂ​ℨ∘\gamma\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}. If γ=0\gamma=0, then ψ∈𝔘n\psi\in\mathfrak{U}_{n}.

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph GG on nn vertices. The exponential of 𝕚​Φ\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi reduces to the finite sum

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=∑ℓ=0κ⁡(Φ)−1𝕚ℓℓ!​Φℓ=𝕀+Ψ,\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=0}^{\kappa(\Phi)-1}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{\ell}}{\ell!}\Phi^{\ell}=\mathbb{I}+\Psi,

where Ψ∈Mat⁡(n,ℂ​ℨn∘)\Psi\in{\rm Mat}(n;{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}}^{\circ}).

Recalling (2.1), the off-diagonal entries of Ψ\Psi satisfy

⟨ζ{i}|Ψ|j⟩=∑I⊆([n]∖∅)𝕚|I|−1​ωI(|I|−1)!​ζI,(i≠j),\langle\zeta_{\{i\}}|\Psi|j\rangle=\sum_{I\subseteq([n]\setminus\varnothing)}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|-1}\omega_{I}}{(|I|-1)!}\zeta_{I},\hskip 12.0pt(i\neq j),

where ωI\omega_{I} is the number of paths in GG from viv_{i} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. Finally, the diagonal entries of Ψ\Psi satisfy

⟨i|Ψ|i⟩=∑I⊆([n]∖∅)𝕚|I|​ξI|I|!​ζI,\langle i|\Psi|i\rangle=\sum_{I\subseteq([n]\setminus\varnothing)}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|}\xi_{I}}{|I|!}\zeta_{I},

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of cycles in GG on vertices indexed by II, and containing viv_{i}.

For convenience, we define the rank-one projector ϖj\varpi_{j} on ℂ​ℨn{\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}}^{n} by ϖj=|j⟩​⟨j|\varpi_{j}=|j\rangle\langle j| for 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n. We further define Δn=diag⁡(ζ{1},…,ζ{n})∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨn)\Delta_{n}={\rm diag}(\zeta_{\{1\}},\ldots,\zeta_{\{n\}})\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}) to be the diagonal matrix whose nonzero entries are the generators of ℂ​ℨn\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}. With these notational preliminaries in mind, we can state our next result.

Theorem 3.6.

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on nn vertices. Then, there exist unique matrices Ψ1∈𝔚n​(ℂ​ℨn)\Psi_{1}\in\mathfrak{W}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}) and Ψ0∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨn∘)\Psi_{0}\in\mathbb{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}}^{\circ}) such that 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=Ψ1+Ψ0\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\Psi_{1}+\Psi_{0}. In particular, Ψ1\Psi_{1} is given by

Ψ1=∑j=1nϖj​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)​ϖj†+Δn​𝔇​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)).\Psi_{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varpi_{j}\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi){\varpi_{j}}^{\dagger}+\Delta_{n}\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)). (3.2)

Moreover, the decomposition is orthogonal:

⟨Ψ0,Ψ1⟩†^=⟨Ψ1,Ψ0⟩†^=0.\langle\Psi_{0},\Psi_{1}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=\langle\Psi_{1},\Psi_{0}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=0.
Proof.

Writing 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=(ϕℓ​j)\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=(\phi_{\ell j}), we see that

∑j=1nϖj​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)​ϖj†=diag⁡(ϕ11,ϕ22,…,ϕn​n),\sum_{j=1}^{n}\varpi_{j}\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi){\varpi_{j}}^{\dagger}={\rm diag}(\phi_{11},\phi_{22},\ldots,\phi_{nn}),

the diagonal matrix whose main diagonal is that of 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi). Further, the matrix Δn​𝔇​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ))\Delta_{n}\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)) is obtained by multiplying the off-diagonal elements of the path matrix by zeon generators corresponding to initial vertices of paths. Since the nilpotent main diagonal elements correspond to cycles, such initial vertices are already accounted for and hence zeroed out by Δn\Delta_{n}. Hence, all nonzero entries of Δn​𝔇​(𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ))\Delta_{n}\mathfrak{D}\mspace{1mu}(\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)) correspond to paths in the graph GG. In accordance with previous results, when i≠ji\neq j,

⟨i|Ψ1|j⟩=∑k=1m∑{I:|I|=k}𝕚|I|−1​ωI(k−1)!ζI\langle i|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\sum_{\{I:|I|=k\}}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|-1}\omega_{I}}{(k-1)!}\zeta_{I}

where ωI\omega_{I} is the number of paths in GG from viv_{i} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. Moreover,

⟨j|Ψ1|j⟩=1+∑k=2n∑{I:|I|=k}𝕚|I|​ξIk!ζI,\langle j|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=1+\sum_{k=2}^{n}\sum_{\{I:|I|=k\}}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|}\xi_{I}}{k!}\zeta_{I},

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of cycles in GG based at vertex vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. To see that Ψ1\Psi_{1} is weakly unitary, we consider the matrix product Ψ1†^​Ψ1{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1}. Writing Ψ1=(yi​j)\Psi_{1}=(y_{ij}), we see that when i≠ji\neq j, the iith row and jjth column of Ψ1†^​Ψ1{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1} is

⟨i|Ψ1†^​Ψ1|j⟩=∑ℓ=1nyℓ​i¯​yℓ​j=0,\langle i|{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\overline{y_{\ell i}}y_{\ell j}=0,

since ζℓ\zeta_{\ell} annihilates each term of yℓ​jy_{\ell j} and yi​ℓy_{i\ell}. Further, diagonal entries of Ψ1†^​Ψ1{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1} are given by

⟨j|Ψ1†^​Ψ1|j⟩=∑ℓ=1nyℓ​j¯​yℓ​j=1+2​∑I𝕚|I|​ξI|I!​ζI,\langle j|{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\overline{y_{\ell j}}y_{\ell j}=1+2\sum_{I}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|}\xi_{I}}{|I!}\zeta_{I},

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of cycles in GG based at vertex vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. Thus, Ψ1†^​Ψ1=𝕀+Γ{\Psi_{1}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1}=\mathbb{I}+\Gamma where Γ\Gamma is a diagonal matrix over ℂ​ℨ∘\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}.

Let Ψ0=𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)−Ψ1=(zi​j)\Psi_{0}=\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)-\Psi_{1}=(z_{ij}). We first observe that zj​j=0z_{jj}=0 for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. Further, for i≠ji\neq j,

⟨i|Ψ0|j⟩=zi​j=(1−ζ{i})∑k=1n∑{I:|I|=k}ωI(k−1)!ζI,\langle i|\Psi_{0}|j\rangle=z_{ij}=(1-\zeta_{\{i\}})\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sum_{\{I:|I|=k\}}\frac{\omega_{I}}{(k-1)!}\zeta_{I},

where ωI\omega_{I} is the number of paths in GG from viv_{i} to vjv_{j} on vertices indexed by II. In particular, zi​j​ζ{j}=0z_{ij}\zeta_{\{j\}}=0 for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. Recalling that ζ{j}​yℓ​j=0\zeta_{\{j\}}y_{\ell j}=0 for ℓ=1,…,n\ell=1,\ldots,n. It follows immediately that

⟨Ψ1,Ψ0⟩†^\displaystyle\langle\Psi_{1},\Psi_{0}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}} =Tr⁡(Ψ0†^​Ψ1)\displaystyle=\Tr({\Psi_{0}}^{\hat{{\dagger}}}\Psi_{1})
=∑j=1n∑ℓ=1nzℓ​j¯​yℓ​j=0.\displaystyle=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\overline{z_{\ell j}}y_{\ell j}=0.

Similar reasoning shows ⟨Ψ0,Ψ1⟩†^=0\langle\Psi_{0},\Psi_{1}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=0. ∎

Remark 3.7.

Vertices of the graph GG are in one-to-one correspondence with states ϖj\varpi_{j} such that ⟨ϖj|Ψ1|ϖj⟩†^\langle\varpi_{j}|\Psi_{1}|\varpi_{j}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}} is the expectation of Ψ1\Psi_{1} in the state ϖj\varpi_{j}. Moreover, this expectation is expressed in terms of the numbers of cycles and their supporting vertices in the graph GG.

As seen in [7], λ∈ℂ​ℨ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z} is an eigenvalue of zeon matrix Ξ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ)\Xi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) if and only if ℭ​λ\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\lambda is a simple zero of the characteristic polynomial of the scalar matrix ℭ⁡(Ξ)\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}(\Xi). If, on the other hand, λ∈ℂ​ℨ\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z} is a zero of χΞ​(u)\chi_{\Xi}(u) and ℭ​λ\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\lambda is a multiple zero of χℭ⁡(Ξ)​(u)\chi_{\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}(\Xi)}(u), then χΞ​(u)\chi_{\Xi}(u) has infinitely many zeon zeros. In particular, we have the following result.

Proposition 3.8.

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on nn vertices. Writing 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=Ψ1+Ψ0\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\Psi_{1}+\Psi_{0} where Ψ1∈𝔚n​(ℂ​ℨn)\Psi_{1}\in\mathfrak{W}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}), it follows that for each j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, the diagonal entry ⟨j|𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)|j⟩=⟨j|Ψ1|j⟩\langle j|\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)|j\rangle=\langle j|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle is a zero of the characteristic polynomial χΨ1​(u)\chi_{\Psi_{1}}(u). Moreover, χΨ1​(u)\chi_{\Psi_{1}}(u) has infinitely many zeon zeros.

Proof.

Fixing j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\} and setting λ=⟨j|Ψ1|j⟩\lambda=\langle j|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle, it is sufficient to show that |λ​𝕀−Ψ1|=0|\lambda\mathbb{I}-\Psi_{1}|=0. Write λ​𝕀−Ψ1=(aℓ​k)\lambda\mathbb{I}-\Psi_{1}=(a_{\ell k}) and consider cofactor expansion in the jjth column:

|λ​𝕀−Ψ1|=|aj​j−a11−a12⋯−a1​j⋯−a1​n−a21aj​j−a22⋯−a2​j⋯−a2​n⋯⋯⋯0⋯−aj​n−an​1−an​2⋯−an​j⋯aj​j−an​n|.|\lambda\mathbb{I}-\Psi_{1}|=\begin{vmatrix}a_{jj}-a_{11}&-a_{12}&\cdots&-a_{1j}&\cdots&-a_{1n}\\ -a_{21}&a_{jj}-a_{22}&\cdots&-a_{2j}&\cdots&-a_{2n}\\ \cdots&\cdots&\cdots&0&\cdots&-a_{jn}\\ -a_{n1}&-a_{n2}&\cdots&-a_{nj}&\cdots&a_{jj}-a_{nn}\end{vmatrix}.

Note that aℓ​ja_{\ell j} annihilates ai​ℓa_{i\ell} for all ℓ≠j\ell\neq j since each is a sum over paths including the common vertex ℓ\ell, and that aj​j=0a_{jj}=0. Hence, all terms of the cofactor expansion of the determinant are zero. ∎

In [6], it was shown that eigenvalues of a graph’s zeon combinatorial Laplacian reveal information about the graph’s cycles. Not surprisingly, eigenvalues of weakly unitary components of nilpotent matrix exponentials can reveal the same information.

Theorem 3.9.

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on nn vertices. Let u=(z1,…,zn)u=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) be a column vector in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that u†​u=1u^{\dagger}u=1 and zi≠zjz_{i}\neq z_{j} for i≠ji\neq j. Let UU denote the rank-one projector u​u†uu^{\dagger} and let 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=Ψ1+Ψ0\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\Psi_{1}+\Psi_{0} be the orthogonal decomposition seen in Theorem 3.6. Then, U​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=U​Ψ1+U​Ψ0U\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=U\Psi_{1}+U\Psi_{0}, where U​Ψ1U\Psi_{1} is a weakly unitary zeon matrix having exactly nn distinct zeon eigenvalues λ1,…,λn∈ℂ​ℨn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}, such that ℭ​λj=zj\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\lambda_{j}=z_{j} for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. Moreover, the eigenvalues of U​Ψ1U\Psi_{1} are precisely the diagonal entries λj=⟨j|U​Ψ1|j⟩\lambda_{j}=\langle j|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle:

λj=zj​⟨j|Ψ1|j⟩=zj​∑I⊆[n]ξI|I|!​ζI,\lambda_{j}=z_{j}\langle j|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=z_{j}\sum_{I\subseteq[n]}\frac{\xi_{I}}{|I|!}\zeta_{I},

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of |I||I|-cycles in GG based at vertex vjv_{j}, on vertices indexed by II.

Proof.

Observing that ℭ⁡(U​Ψ1)=U\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}(U\Psi_{1})=U, it follows that U​Ψ1U\Psi_{1} has nn distinct zeon eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n} whose scalar parts are ℭ​λj=zj\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}\lambda_{j}=z_{j} for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n.

Write 𝔄=U​Ψ1=(ai​j)\mathfrak{A}=U\Psi_{1}=(a_{ij}), so that ai​j=⟨i|U​Ψ1|j⟩a_{ij}=\langle i|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle. Fixing j∈{1,…,n}j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}, consider the determinant

χ𝔄​(aj​j)\displaystyle\chi_{\mathfrak{A}}(a_{jj}) =|aj​j​𝕀−𝔄|\displaystyle=|a_{jj}\mathbb{I}-\mathfrak{A}|
=|aj​j−a11−a12−a13⋯⋯−a1​n−a21aj​j−a22−a23⋯⋯−a2​n⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯−aj​1−aj​2⋯0⋯−aj​n⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯⋯−an​1−an​2⋯⋯⋯aj​j−an​n|.\displaystyle=\begin{vmatrix}a_{jj}-a_{11}&-a_{12}&-a_{13}&\cdots&\cdots&-a_{1n}\\ -a_{21}&a_{jj}-a_{22}&-a_{23}&\cdots&\cdots&-a_{2n}\\ \cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\\ -a_{j1}&-a_{j2}&\cdots&0&\cdots&-a_{jn}\\ \cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&\\ -a_{n1}&-a_{n2}&\cdots&\cdots&\cdots&a_{jj}-a_{nn}\end{vmatrix}.

Computing the determinant by cofactor expansion in the jjth row, we note first that the cofactor of 0 is determined by the only invertible minor in the determinant. All other summands in the cofactor expansion are nilpotent. Secondly, we note that ζ{ℓ}​aj​ℓ=0\zeta_{\{\ell\}}a_{j\ell}=0 for each ℓ\ell because terms of aj​ℓa_{j\ell} represent paths from vjv_{j} to vℓv_{\ell} in GG. Computing the cofactor (−1)j+ℓ​|𝔄j​ℓ^|(-1)^{j+\ell}|\widehat{\mathfrak{A}_{j\ell}}| by cofactor expansion of the minor in row ℓ\ell, we further see that ζ{ℓ}​|𝔄j​ℓ^|=0\zeta_{\{\ell\}}|\widehat{\mathfrak{A}_{j\ell}}|=0. Hence, (−1)j+ℓ​aj​ℓ​|𝔄j​ℓ^|=0(-1)^{j+\ell}a_{j\ell}|\widehat{\mathfrak{A}_{j\ell}}|=0 for each ℓ=1,…,n\ell=1,\ldots,n.

We conclude that χ𝔄​(aj​j)=|aj​j​𝕀−𝔄|=0\chi_{\mathfrak{A}}(a_{jj})=|a_{jj}\mathbb{I}-\mathfrak{A}|=0 for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, so that the eigenvalues of 𝔄=U​Ψ1\mathfrak{A}=U\Psi_{1} are precisely λj=aj​j\lambda_{j}=a_{jj}. ∎

Remark 3.10.

As was the case in Theorem 3.6, U​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=U​Ψ1+U​Ψ0U\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=U\Psi_{1}+U\Psi_{0} is an orthogonal decomposition; i.e., ⟨U​Ψ1,U​Ψ0⟩†^=0\langle U\Psi_{1},U\Psi_{0}\rangle_{\hat{{\dagger}}}=0.

In the next theorem, an approach is offered to obtain an eigenvalue of Ψ1\Psi_{1} while only concerning ourselves with real zeon matrices, i.e., matrices in 𝕄n​(ℨn)\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathfrak{Z}_{n}).

Theorem 3.11.

Let Φ\Phi be the nilpotent adjacency matrix of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on nn vertices. Let U=diag⁡(z1,…,zn)∈{±1}nU={\rm diag}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} be a diagonal matrix satisfying zj=1z_{j}=1 for some j∈[n]j\in[n] and zℓ=−1z_{\ell}=-1 for ℓ≠j\ell\neq j, and let 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=Ψ1+Ψ0\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\Psi_{1}+\Psi_{0} be the orthogonal decomposition seen in Theorem 3.6. Then, U​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=U​Ψ1+U​Ψ0U\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=U\Psi_{1}+U\Psi_{0}, where U​Ψ1U\Psi_{1} is a weakly unitary zeon matrix having unique eigenvalue λj=⟨j|U​Ψ1|j⟩=⟨j|Ψ1|j⟩∈ℂ​ℨn\lambda_{j}=\langle j|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=\langle j|\Psi_{1}|j\rangle\in\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}. This eigenvalue is also a zero of the characteristic polynomial of Ψ1\Psi_{1} and is given by

λj=∑I⊆[n]𝕚|I|​ξI|I|!​ζI,\lambda_{j}=\sum_{I\subseteq[n]}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|}\xi_{I}}{|I|!}\zeta_{I},

where ξI\xi_{I} is the number of |I||I|-cycles in GG based at vertex vjv_{j}, on vertices indexed by II. Moreover, a unit right eigenvector |μ⟩=(μ1,…,1⏟j​th pos,…​μn)⊺|\mu\rangle=(\mu_{1},\ldots,\underset{j\text{\rm th pos}}{\underbrace{1}},\ldots\mu_{n})^{\intercal} is given by

μℓ=−12⟨ℓ|UΨ1|j⟩=−12∑I⊆[n]𝕚|I|−1​ωI(|I|−1)!ζI,\mu_{\ell}=-\frac{1}{2}\langle\ell|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{I\subseteq[n]}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{|I|-1}\omega_{I}}{(|I|-1)!}\zeta_{I},

where ωI\omega_{I} denotes the number of paths from vℓv_{\ell} to vjv_{j} in GG on vertices indexed by II.

Proof.

The fact that λj\lambda_{j} is an eigenvalue follows from the proof of Theorem 3.9. Proceeding to the characterization of the associated eigenvector, let |μ⟩=(μ1,…,1,…,μn)⊺|\mu\rangle=(\mu_{1},\ldots,1,\ldots,\mu_{n})^{\intercal} as stated above, and let us consider U​Ψ1​|μ⟩U\Psi_{1}|\mu\rangle. Note that paths k→ℓk\to\ell and paths ℓ→j\ell\to j are annihilated by ζℓ\zeta_{\ell}, so it follows that ⟨k|U​Ψ1|ℓ⟩​⟨ℓ|U​Ψ1|j⟩=0\langle k|U\Psi_{1}|\ell\rangle\langle\ell|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle=0 when ℓ≠j\ell\neq j. Thus, the kkth component of U​Ψ1​𝐯U\Psi_{1}\mathbf{v} is given by

⟨k|U​Ψ1|μ⟩\displaystyle\langle k|U\Psi_{1}|\mu\rangle =λj​⟨k|U​Ψ1​|j⟩+12​∑ℓ≠j⟨k|​U​Ψ1|ℓ⟩​⟨ℓ|U​Ψ1|j⟩\displaystyle=\lambda_{j}\langle k|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell\neq j}\langle k|U\Psi_{1}|\ell\rangle\langle\ell|U\Psi_{1}|j\rangle
=λj​μk,\displaystyle=\lambda_{j}\mu_{k},

which shows that U​Ψ1​|μ⟩=λj​|μ⟩U\Psi_{1}|\mu\rangle=\lambda_{j}|\mu\rangle. ∎

Hadamard Decomposition

Observing that each zeon generator can be written as a product of disjoint fermion annihilators (or creators), we have an obvious decomposition of the nilpotent adjacency matrix into an Hadamard product of fermion adjacency matrices.

Letting 𝔉\mathfrak{F} denote the algebra of fermion annihilators generated by {fi:i∈ℕ}\{f_{i}:i\in\mathbb{N}\}, zeon generators can be defined by ζ{j}=f2​j−1​f2​j\zeta_{\{j\}}=f_{2j-1}f_{2j} for j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}. The nilpotent adjacency matrix Φ\Phi of a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) on nn vertices can then be written as the Hadamard product of two fermion adjacency matrices associated with GG. In particular, Φ=Φ1⊙Φ2\Phi=\Phi_{1}\odot\Phi_{2}, where Φ1\Phi_{1} and Φ2\Phi_{2} are determined by

⟨i|Φ1|j⟩={f2​j−1{vi,vj}∈E,0otherwise,\displaystyle\langle i|\Phi_{1}|j\rangle=\begin{cases}f_{2j-1}&\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\in E,\\ 0&\text{\rm otherwise,}\end{cases}\hskip 12.0pt ⟨i|Φ2|j⟩={f2​j{vi,vj}∈E,0otherwise.\displaystyle\langle i|\Phi_{2}|j\rangle=\begin{cases}f_{2j}&\{v_{i},v_{j}\}\in E,\\ 0&\text{\rm otherwise.}\end{cases}

It is well known22 2 See, for example, [2]. that the Hadamard product is related to the Kronecker product by

Φ1⊙Φ2=J⁡(Φ1⊗Φ2)​J†,\Phi_{1}\odot\Phi_{2}=J(\Phi_{1}\otimes\Phi_{2})J^{\dagger},

where JJ is an appropriately constructed selection matrix. When Φ1,Φ2\Phi_{1},\Phi_{2} are square matrices of order nn, JJ is the n×n2n\times n^{2} matrix

J=(𝐞1𝐞n+2𝐞2​n+3⋯𝐞n2)⊺,J=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{e}_{1}&\mathbf{e}_{n+2}&\mathbf{e}_{2n+3}&\cdots&\mathbf{e}_{n^{2}}\end{pmatrix}^{\intercal},

whose nn rows 𝐞j\mathbf{e}_{j} are unit coordinate vectors of ℂn2\mathbb{C}^{n^{2}}.

The nilpotent (zeon) adjacency matrix is then written in terms of fermion adjacency matrices via Φ=J⁡(Φ1⊗Φ2)​J†\Phi=J(\Phi_{1}\otimes\Phi_{2})J^{\dagger}. It is worth noting that J†​JJ^{\dagger}J is a rank-nn orthogonal projection.

Letting Θ=J†​J​(Φ1⊗Φ2)\Theta=J^{\dagger}J(\Phi_{1}\otimes\Phi_{2}), we find that for each positive integer m≥2m\geq 2,

Φm\displaystyle\Phi^{m} =(J⁡(Φ1⊗Φ2)​J†)m\displaystyle=(J(\Phi_{1}\otimes\Phi_{2})J^{\dagger})^{m}
=J​Θm​J†.\displaystyle=J\Theta^{m}J^{\dagger}.

Hence,

𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)=∑ℓ=0κ⁡(Φ)𝕚ℓℓ!​Φℓ\displaystyle\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\kappa(\Phi)}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{\ell}}{\ell!}\Phi^{\ell} =∑ℓ=0κ⁡(Φ)𝕚ℓℓ!​J​Θℓ​J†\displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=0}^{\kappa(\Phi)}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{\ell}}{\ell!}J\Theta^{\ell}J^{\dagger}
=J⁡(∑ℓ=0κ⁡(Φ)𝕚ℓℓ!​Θℓ)​J†\displaystyle=J\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{\kappa(\Phi)}\frac{\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}^{\ell}}{\ell!}\Theta^{\ell}\right)J^{\dagger}
=J​𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Θ)​J†.\displaystyle=J\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Theta)J^{\dagger}.

4 Concluding Remarks

The motivation for considering unitary and weakly unitary zeon matrices is twofold. First, they arise naturally as exponentials of nilpotent adjacency matrices. Second, they provide zeon-algebraic analogues of unitary operators, which are of particular importance in quantum probability and quantum computation. Some avenues of further exploration follow.

Zeon Matrix Groups

The preliminary investigation of unitary zeon matrices leads to a much larger problem of classifying the various zeon matrix groups and subgroups. As we have seen, the groups 𝔘n\mathfrak{U}_{n}, 𝔚n\mathfrak{W}_{n}, and 𝔊n\mathfrak{G}_{n} satisfy 𝔘n≤𝔚n≤𝔊n\mathfrak{U}_{n}\leq\mathfrak{W}_{n}\leq\mathfrak{G}_{n}. Further, the group ℑn={𝕀+Ψ:Ψ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)}≤𝔊n\mathfrak{I}_{n}=\{\mathbb{I}+\Psi:\Psi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ})\}\leq\mathfrak{G}_{n}.

The relationships among zeon matrix groups, including chains and lattices, are yet to be investigated. The relationships among weakly unitary matrices obtained from orthogonal decompositions of nilpotent adjacency matrix exponentials could be interesting–particularly from a graph-theoretic perspective.

Zeon Lie Theory

The algebra 𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}) of nilpotent zeon matrices constitutes a Lie algebra with the bracket [X,Y]=X​Y−Y​X[X,Y]=XY-YX. The exponential map 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭:𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)→𝔊n​(ℂ​ℨ)\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}:\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ})\to\mathfrak{G}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}) then satisfies 𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(X)=𝕀+Ψ\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(X)=\mathbb{I}+\Psi where Ψ∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)\Psi\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}). In fact, the scalar part of the determinant satisfies ℭ⁡(|𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(X)|)=1\mathfrak{C}\mspace{1mu}(|\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(X)|)=1 for every X∈𝕄n​(ℂ​ℨ∘)X\in\mathbb{M}_{n}(\mathbb{C}\mathfrak{Z}^{\circ}).

For any nilpotent adjacency matrix Φ\Phi, the exponential map satisfies |𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Φ)|=1|\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Phi)|=1. Moreover, given any linear combination Ψ=∑j=1maj​Φj\Psi=\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\Phi_{j} of nilpotent adjacency matrices, it can be shown that |𝔢​𝔵​𝔭​(𝕚​Ψ)|=1|\mathfrak{exp}\mspace{1mu}(\mathbbm{i}\mspace{1mu}\Psi)|=1. One obvious question is: What can be said about Lie groups in this context?
